South Korea just bet $880 billion on AI.

Not on software. Not on models. On the physical infrastructure that makes everything else run — AI chips and data centers at a scale no single nation has committed before.

Two anchor companies are driving roughly $500 billion of that number. South Korea already controls the advanced memory chip market through Samsung and SK hynix. This commitment extends that dominance across the full AI compute stack.

Why this matters beyond the headline: the infrastructure layer of AI is now a multi-polar competition. The U.S. is building. The Gulf states are building. South Korea is building. Each at trillion-dollar scale.

For business leaders, this creates a new strategic reality. Multiple competing compute ecosystems mean more options, better pricing, and greater supply chain resilience. But only for organizations that architect their AI infrastructure strategy to span these geographies instead of depending on any single one.

The companies that navigate this well will have a structural cost and resilience advantage for the next decade.
